title: Comm-slicing and token-stripe scheduler for asymmetric multi-GPU inference
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: For heterogeneous instance shapes and mixed sequence-length workloads we observe latency spikes and suboptimal GPU utilization during prefill and decode. Current mgpu conductor batches whole-tokens per-stage which amplifies NCCL stalls when a single slow stage or large KV cache fetch blocks global collectives.

Proposal: Implement a two-part runtime scheduler: (1) comm-slicing - break large NCCL collectives (allreduce/allgather/collectives used during KV sync and attention recompute) into overlapping micro-collectives (slices) that can be pipelined with compute and upstream token work to increase NCCL overlap; (2) token-stripe scheduling - instead of assigning contiguous token ranges per device, stripe tokens across devices in small stripes (e.g., 16-64 token stripes) and schedule compute+comm for stripes opportunistically based on per-stage readiness and kernel selection heuristics.

Key ideas and signals: use per-kernel latency estimates, recent-sequence-length histogram, and current KV cache hotness to decide slice sizes and stripe widths. Allow asymmetric slice widths per-connection to adapt to heterogeneous interconnect speed (e.g., NVLink vs PCIe fabrics). Integrate with kernel-selection hooks to prefer compute kernels that free the GPU earlier when a pending comm slice is expected (trade compute efficiency vs parallelism).

Why different: Unlike previous global overlap approaches, this design explicitly trades deterministic per-token compute cost for smoother end-to-end latency by increasing parallelism at the communication grain and allowing asymmetric scheduling across devices. It targets worst-case tail latency and bursty request patterns rather than steady-state throughput alone.
acceptance_criteria:
1) End-to-end p99 latency for mixed-length chat workload reduces by >=18% vs baseline without sacrificing p50 by >5%.
2) GPU utilization increase on average by >=12% across heterogeneous cluster tests.
3) No correctness regressions: generated outputs identical (bit-for-bit) for deterministic modes; probabilistic modes within existing fidelity thresholds.
4) Unit tests for comm-slicing state machine and stripe allocator added with >=90% branch coverage.
5) Feature gate present with rollout flags and per-customer knob for slice size / stripe width.
risks_and_mitigation:
Risk: Slicing collectives can increase total bytes moved and lead to perf regression on high-bandwidth low-latency fabrics if slice size too small. Mitigation: autotune slice size using short microbenchmarks per machine and fallback to single-collective for small models.
Risk: Token striping may complicate KV cache locality and increase memory pressure. Mitigation: implement adaptive stripe placement that preserves hot-token co-location for known long-context prefixes.
Risk: Debugging race conditions in comm state machine. Mitigation: deterministic debug mode that serializes comm steps and a simulator harness for replaying schedules.
metrics: Baseline targets and measurement plan: p50/p95/p99 token latencies, GPU SM utilization, NCCL activity overlap ratio (time spent in comm while compute active), bytes-per-second per-link, end-to-end cost-per-token delta. Dashboards: runtime-perf/eng/comm-slicing (provisioned), and perf/regression alerts tied to 2x weekly evaluation harness.
implementation_notes:
Phases: (A) prototype comm-slicing in runtime's comm layer with a configurable slice_count and per-collective policy; perf microbench on representative instances. (B) add token-stripe allocator in scheduler with stripe size heuristic and integration point for kernel selection hints; simulate with synthetic workload driver. (C) combine with kernel-selection hooks and add autotune job that runs during node bootstrap. (D) controlled rollout behind feature flag with canary traffic.
Key files/areas: runtime/comm/* (new slice manager), scheduler/stripe_allocator.cpp, kernels/hint_interface.h, tests/mgpu/slice_simulator.cc.
Compatibility: must interoperate with existing NCCL and non-NCCL paths (e.g., custom RPC-based comm for private deployments). Provide fallback to previous conductor on feature-off.
